one_liner: Header-only C++17 kd-tree for exact and approximate kNN, radius and box search; builds faster than nanoflann and OpenCV FLANN.
what_it_does: PicoTree builds a static kd-tree over 2D/3D (or run-time-dimension) point sets and answers nearest-neighbour, k-nearest, radius and axis-aligned box queries, plus approximate (1+e) variants and custom search visitors. Point sets plug in through space/point traits: std::vector of arrays, raw contiguous buffers via space_map, Eigen matrices and cv::Mat are supported out of the box. Besides L1, squared L2 and L-infinity it has metrics for spaces with wrap-around (SO(2) on the circle, squared SE(2)), and it ships pybind11 Python bindings that take NumPy arrays. The API (pico_tree::kd_tree<Space, Metric, Index>, search_knn/search_radius/search_box) is not a drop-in for nanoflann's adaptor interface.
how_it_is_fast: The default split rule is sliding midpoint (Maneewongvatana and Mount, 'It's okay to be skinny, if your friends are fat'): it cuts the longest box side at its middle with a linear std::partition and falls back to std::nth_element only when one side would be empty, which avoids median selection at every level. During construction each leaf's box is shrunk to the points it holds, and the parent stores the actual left-child max and right-child min on the split axis, so queries pick the nearer child from the real gap and prune with tighter bounds. Nearest-neighbour search uses Arya-Mount incremental distance calculation (only the split-axis term of the box distance is updated per step) with non-square-rooted metrics. Nodes come from a pool allocator in chunks of 256 rather than per-node new or std::deque, and fixing the dimension at compile time lets the distance loops unroll.
when_to_use: Static 3D point clouds (LiDAR scans, ICP correspondence search) where the tree is rebuilt often: on the author's 7.7M-point scan a single-threaded build took 0.54 s vs 0.99 s for OpenCV FLANN and 1.42 s reported for nanoflann 1.7.1
Single-nearest-neighbour or small-k queries over millions of query points in C++: knn=1 took 1.13 s vs 1.40 s (nanoflann) and 2.30 s (OpenCV FLANN) for 7.2M queries

Python pipelines that need exact kNN on NumPy float arrays: knn=1 took 1.64 s vs 2.95 s for pykdtree, 11.9 s for scikit-learn and 212 s for SciPy KDTree in the README, and the bindings can parallelize queries with OpenMP
Data already in Eigen matrices, cv::Mat or a flat float buffer, used without copying (pass a std::reference_wrapper or space_map)
Robotics or planar problems with angular coordinates (SO(2), SE(2)) where the metric has to wrap around
when_not_to_use: Point sets that change: builds are static only, with no insert or remove. Use nanoflann's dynamic/incremental adaptors or Pkd-tree for batch updates
Build-dominated workloads on multi-core machines: construction is single-threaded, while nanoflann 1.5+ has n_thread_build and Pkd-tree builds in parallel
High-dimensional approximate search (descriptors, embeddings): only the (1+e) kd-tree approximation and an example KdForest exist, so FAISS or an HNSW library is a better fit
pip-only Python environments: there is no PyPI package (pypi.org/pypi/pico_tree returns 404), so you build from source with scikit-build, pybind11 and OpenMP
Projects that need an actively maintained dependency: the last commit is 2025-08-10, there are 49 stars, and the 7 issues ever filed are all closed

integration.dependencies: none for the C++ core; Eigen and OpenCV are optional (traits headers only); Python bindings need pybind11, NumPy, OpenMP and scikit-build (Python 3.10+); Google Benchmark, nanoflann and OpenCV only for the benchmarks; Google Test for the unit tests
integration.min_toolchain: C++17 (issue #32: does not compile with GCC 7.5 on Ubuntu 18.04); CMake 3.12+ if you use the CMake package rather than copying src/pico_tree
integration.platforms: any; no SIMD intrinsics. CI builds on the latest macOS, Ubuntu and Windows runners
integration.thread_safety: README lists 'Thread safe queries': the search methods are const, so many threads can query one built tree. Construction is single-threaded. The Python bindings run queries over the input array with OpenMP (set OMP_NUM_THREADS to control it)

gotchas: With the default metric_l2_squared, radius inputs and all returned distances are squared, and approximate-search error ratios must be squared too (pass tree.metric()(1 + e))

The tree takes the point set by value: pass std::move(points) or a std::reference_wrapper to avoid a copy. The tree holds pointers into its node pool, so it is move-only, and a referenced point set must outlive it and stay unchanged
The default index type is int (32-bit signed). Query and tree scalar types must match exactly (a double query against a float tree fails to compile), and an empty input is caught only by assert
save/load is a same-machine convenience: no endianness handling, no check that the stored tree matches the point set or template arguments, and the point set itself is not saved
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick PicoTree over nanoflann when you rebuild static trees often on one thread, need box search or wrap-around metrics, or want NumPy bindings in the same package. Pick nanoflann when you need dynamic insert/remove, a multi-threaded build, distro/vcpkg/Conan packaging or active maintenance. picoflann, Janos95/kdtree and kd3 make similar nanoflann-beating claims but cover fewer query types.
verified_claims_summary: The author's README table compares PicoTree v1.0.0 with nanoflann 1.7.1 and OpenCV FLANN 4.11.0 (C++), and with SciPy 1.15.2, scikit-learn 1.6.1 and pykdtree 1.3.7 (Python), on an Intel Core i9-14900HX: one thread, max_leaf_size=10, knn=1, a 7,733,372-point Bremen LiDAR cloud to build and a 7,200,863-point cloud to query. The compiler and flags are not stated. PicoTree is 1.2x faster than nanoflann at knn and 2.0x faster than OpenCV FLANN, and it builds 1.8x faster than OpenCV FLANN. The 2.6x build gap against nanoflann is inflated: since nanoflann 1.4 its KDTreeSingleIndexAdaptor constructor already calls buildIndex(), and examples/benchmark/bm_nanoflann.cpp then calls tree.buildIndex() again inside the timed loop, so nanoflann's 1.42 s covers two builds. That matches the '90% slower in nanoflann v1.5.0' note in docs/benchmark.md. Halving it suggests about a 1.3x real gap (derived estimate, not measured). In Python, pykdtree builds faster (0.43 s vs 0.54 s).
status_note: Stale (last commit 2025-08-10, v1.0.0 is the latest release, 49 stars) but MIT-licensed, header-only and small enough to vendor by copying src/pico_tree; the Python bindings must be built from source.
